newsitem.title: UK: EMU opt-out won't scupper UK investment - economists.
newsitem.headline: EMU opt-out won't scupper UK investment - economists.

text.p: Britain is unlikely to be shunned by global companies if it stays out of a single European currency despite a growing chorus of multinationals urging a more pro-integration stance, economists said on Thursday.

A British newspaper on Thursday reported British Aerospace (BAe) chief executive Sir Richard Evans said a single currency as "pretty damn fundamental for European industry" and warned Britain not to adopt an isolationist stance in Europe.
"We are very much in favour of being an integral part of Europe. What is important to us is stability of currencies," The Guardian quoted him as saying.

His comments followed recent warnings by Anglo-Dutch conglomerate Unilever and Japanese car maker Toyota that they could move their European investments elsewhere if Britain stayed out of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
But economists said Britain could continue to attract investment even if it chooses not to sign up for a single currency.

"There is certainly an argument that if we don't join EMU and the rest of Europe signs up to it, there could be a detrimental effect to some degree," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"But I don't think you should overstate the case. There are more important considerations than the single currency, because currency movements can be hedged," he said. "Companies also look at labour markets, tax breaks and so on, and Britain may have an advantage there over France and Germany."
Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International, said staying out of EMU would have little impact on investment.

"What you would lose in benefits from a single currency, which are lack of volatility in exchange rates, you gain in the ability to do what you want with your own monetary policy," he said. "It by no means follows that what is applicable for BAe is indicative of the overall corporate sector in the UK."

Carr said that although most companies would be unruffled if Britain stayed out of EMU, they would reconsider investing in the country if an EMU opt-out heralded a move towards a more isolationist stance.
"What companies fear is not Britain staying out of a single currency but Britain becoming more isolated in Europe. Isolation would damage investment," he said.
But Richardson said Britain could gain by maintaining its distance from the rest of Europe.
"Analogies of the Hong Kong of Europe have been made and they are not without their merits," he said.

"If you are a country which sits on the edge of a landmass like Europe which is bogged down by labour market inefficiencies and rigidities, and you have flexible exchange rates and can set your own monetary policy, then you could very well benefit."

Britain's opposition Labour Party, however, said an isolationist stance could cost thousands of jobs. Labour is gearing up for a general election which must be held by May 22, and leads the Conservative government of Prime Minister John Major in the polls.
"It is becoming increasingly clear that Mr Major's willingness to pander to the Eurosceptics is causing very loud alarm bells to ring within leading companies," Labour's Brian Wilson said.
"There are tens of thousands of jobs at stake if Britain's role in Europe continues to be a pawn in the internal warfare of the Tory party."
Both the Labour and the Conservatives have declined to commit themselves to joining EMU in the first wave.
